summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for network management protocols, with objects for managing networks that use the Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Network gear keeps a list of gauges and settings that managers can read. This document defines the gauges for tunnels made with L2TP.

subtitle: The SNMP objects that let network managers configure and monitor L2TP tunnels and sessions.

tldr.problem: Operators who run Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) devices need a standard way to configure, watch and count their tunnels and sessions with network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SNMP MIB module, L2TP-MIB, with configuration and statistics tables for domains, tunnels and sessions, plus a mapping table and one notification, and ties tunnels into the Interfaces MIB.
tldr.outcome: Different vendors' L2TP gear can be managed the same way. Write access and shared secrets need SNMP protection, and the RFC recommends SNMPv3 security.

today: RFC 3371 is a Proposed Standard from September 2002. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and the SNMP Framework
sections.content:
RFC 3371 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing L2TP devices. A MIB is a virtual information store, and its objects are defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI).

The module is written in SMIv2. A SMIv1 version can be produced by translation and should be semantically equivalent, except for objects omitted because no translation is possible, such as those using Counter64. The RFC lists the parts of the SNMP Management Framework: an architecture, the SMI, message protocols (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, SNMPv3), protocol operations, and fundamental applications with view-based access control.
sections.plainLanguage: Managers use a shared list of named gauges to look at network machines. This document adds gauges for L2TP tunnels.

sections.title: Overview of the Seven Groups
sections.content:
The MIB is built from seven groups of objects for L2TP tunnels, as defined in RFC 2661.

  • l2tpConfigGroup and l2tpStatsGroup: configuration, state and statistics for the protocol, its tunnels and sessions. Mandatory.
  • l2tpDomainGroup: optional; covers tunnel endpoint domains, which are collections of L2TP devices typically sharing an administrative domain or location.
  • l2tpMappingGroup: optional mapping tables to relate protocol identifiers and table indices.
  • l2tpIpUdpGroup: state and statistics for tunnels carried over UDP/IP. Mandatory for implementations that support L2TP over UDP/IP.
  • l2tpSecurityGroup: optional, for agents that support both authentication and privacy of SNMP messages, for managing L2TP keys.
  • l2tpTrapGroup: the notifications an implementation can generate.
  • l2tpHCPacketGroup: optional, for implementations whose 32-bit domain counters could overflow in less than an hour.
sections.plainLanguage: The gauges are sorted into seven drawers. Two drawers must always be there, and the rest are for extra features.

sections.title: Relationship to the Interfaces MIB
sections.content:
The MIB extends the IP Tunnel MIB (RFC 2667), which itself extends the Interfaces MIB (RFC 2863). An L2TP tunnel is represented as its own logical interface sub-layer with ifType tunnel(131). Implementing the IP Tunnel MIB is required for L2TP tunnels over IP.

On an L2TP Network Server (LNS), the tunnel is not at the top of the interface stack: PPP interfaces are layered on top of it, and the RFC's example shows four PPP interfaces on one tunnel, two of them under a multilink PPP interface. On an L2TP Access Concentrator (LAC), tunnel interfaces appear at the top of the stack.

The RFC also says how Interfaces MIB objects behave for tunnels. For UDP/IP transport, ifMtu should be 65467 (65535 minus 60 for IP minus 8 for UDP). ifSpeed returns zero. Setting ifAdminStatus to up injects a Local Open request into the tunnel state machine, and down injects a Tunnel Close event. Packet and octet counters include both control and payload traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel is treated like another network plug on the machine. Counters for it count both the tunnel's own chatter and the real data.

sections.title: Tables for Domains, Tunnels and Sessions
sections.content:
Section 4 holds the MIB module itself, L2TP-MIB. It starts with scalars: l2tpAdminState (enabled or disabled; disabling immediately disconnects all tunnels and stops new ones) and l2tpDrainTunnels (stops new tunnels and sessions without disconnecting active ones). Read-only scalars report supported protocol versions, vendor name, firmware revision and whether draining is under way.

Then come configuration and statistics tables. A domain table pair covers an endpoint or group of endpoints, with settings such as the authentication mode (none, simple or challenge), tunnel security (none, other or ipSec), hello interval (default 60 seconds, zero disables hellos) and idle timeout, plus counters for tunnels, sessions and traffic, with high-capacity versions. Per-tunnel configuration and statistics tables mirror these settings and add remote host name, vendor, last result and error codes. A session statistics table tracks each session's identifiers, user name, call type, connect speeds and framing.

The l2tpSessionMapTable lets a management application find which session an interface maps to. On a LAC it also maps a physical or virtual interface that ends a PPP link to a tunnel, which is needed because interface stacking cannot be used at the LAC.
sections.plainLanguage: There are lists for each group of machines, each tunnel and each call inside a tunnel. Each list has settings you can change and counters you can read.

sections.title: Tunnel and Session States, and Notifications
sections.content:
Tunnel state is reported in l2tpTunnelStatsState and session state in l2tpSessionStatsState. Both use four values: idle, connecting, established and disconnecting.

Creating a tunnel entry in the IP Tunnel MIB when the encapsulation is l2tp has the side effect of creating entries in the L2TP tunnel configuration and statistics tables and the UDP statistics tables. Creating tunnels over non-IP transports is left to the MIB for that transport.

The only generic notification is l2tpTunnelAuthFailure, sent when an attempt to establish a tunnel to a remote peer fails authentication. It carries whether the tunnel was initiated locally and the remote host name.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tunnel and each call is always in one of four moods: not started, starting, working, or ending. One alarm rings if a visitor fails the password check.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Reading the MIB is described as relatively innocuous. Writable objects are the risk: unauthorized access could cause denial of service or unauthorized creation and manipulation of tunnels. SNMPv1 by itself is an insecure environment, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may SET objects.

Keys such as l2tpDomainConfigSecret are only as safe as SNMP. All objects in the l2tpSecurityGroup MUST NOT be accessible via unencrypted messages, and the RFC recommends that keys not be visible through GET, GET-NEXT or GET-BULK even with encryption. In the shared-secret object, the agent MUST report an empty string in response to reads. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with the User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control Model, and makes it the user's responsibility to configure access properly.
sections.plainLanguage: Looking at gauges is mostly safe, but turning knobs or reading the secret password is not. So only trusted people with locked-down connections should be allowed to do that.
